TESTIMONY IN FAVOR OF LD 321
PROGRESSIVE SUPRANUCLEAR PALSY ANACT T0 MAKE MAY MONTH
February 24, 2025

Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, honorable members of the Joint Standing
Committee on State and Local Govermnent. I am Jack Ducharme, and I have the honor
of representing the citizens of Maine House District 71 which includes the towns of
Cornville, Noiridgewock, and Madison in Somerset County. I am here today to introduce
my bill, LD 321, An Act to make the month of May Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
Month. I am submitting this bill at the request of a friend, formerly of Madison, whose
wife is afflicted with this insidious disease.

Lee and Glenda Longe, formerly of Madison, now living in Georgia, worked all their
lives to be successful in Maine. Lee was a papennalcer, Glenda worked at the local I-Iannaford. Circumstances including the closure of Madison Paper in 2016 led them to
eventually move to Georgia to be closer to family there. Glenda was diagnosed with Progressive Supranuclear Palsy while in Georgia after many doctors visits. Lee has
submitted his written testimony that details the specifics of Glenda's affliction, so I will
not recount that here.

Progressive Supranucieax Palsy (PSP) is a rare and debilitating neurodegenerative disorder that affects movement, balance, speech, and cognitive function. In Maine, as in
many other regions, awareness of PSP is limited, leading to delays in diagnosis and a lack of suppoit for those affected. PSP can be challenging to diagnose as its symptoms overlap with other neurological conditions, such as Parkinson's disease. There is no cLu`e for PSP, but treatments can help manage symptoms and improve quality of life.

PSP is a progressive condition, and symptoms typically worsen over time. The average life expectancy after diagnosis is around 7~10 years, although some individuals may live
longer.

Designating May as Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Month in Maine would serve several
important purposes:

� Raise Awareness: A dedicated month would help educate the public about PSP,
its symptoms, and its impact on individuals and families. o Support Research: Increased awareness can lead to greater funding and support
for research aimed at finding effective treatments and, ultimately, a cure. - Provide Support: Highlighting PSP can connect patients and caregivers with
resources, support groups, and healthcare professionals experienced in managing
the disease.
In 2024, the U.S. House of Representatives passed H.Res.1260, expressing support for
designating May as "Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Awareness Month." This national
recognition underscores the importance of raising awareness and supporting those
affected by PSP. In May 2024, the Commonwealth of Virginia passed a resolution naming May Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Month of Awareness for 2024 and in each
succeeding year. I understand that similar legislation is being considered in Vermont and
other states.

Designating May as Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Month provides an opportunity for
all Mainers to learn more about progressive supranuclear palsy and seek Ways to support research into treatment and cures or to provide hope and assistance to people living with
the disease and their families. By adopting a similar designation in Maine, we can join a broader movement to support individuals with PSP and their families, ensuring they
receive the attention and care they deserve.

Thank you for your consideration of this legislation. I am happy to answer any questions that you may have to the extent that I am able.

Written Testimony for Maine LD321 - A Resolution to Make the month of May Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Month:
Thank you Rep Ducharme for bring the Resolution to Make May Progressive Supranuclear Palsy Month in Maine and to the Committee for this time. I am Jan Appel. I live in Vermont in a town just north of Burlington and near where Lee Longe grew up. Vermont, like Maine, is a rural state without large research facilities or PSP Centers of Care. I am here today to honor my husband, Ken who died 7 years ago in March and to support Lee Longe's request for this Resolution. Lee and I met through CurePSP, an organization focused on PSP and Lee and I are also working to have Vermont adopt a similar resolution as the one before you today. I am here to share my experience with PSP as each person with the disease and each family's experience is similar but unique and this is a factor in making communities aware of this horrible disease
Ken was a skilled attorney who loved the law and fought hard on behalf of his clients. He was really smart, highly competitive, determined to win whether a game of chess or a case in court. Ken liked to live life to the fullest. He loved Mountain biking. Ken was diagnosed with PSP in December 2016, 14 months before his death, by a neurologist whose specialty was MS. However, she was extremely knowledgeable as she had done all her post medical school training at Mayo in MN under experts regarding these diseases. Our journey to diagnosis was the result of an OT who had been on his care team for each of the 5 orthopedic surgeries Ken had in the prior year for what we later recognized were actually related to be PSP symptoms.
At the time of his diagnosis, I had been struggling for years to understand the significant physical and emotional changes he presented. After his death as I dismantled his law office, I recognized that symptoms had begun much earlier than I was aware. The disease had progressed slowly, gaining speed over time. The presentation and understanding of what was happening to him was complicated by his mental and physical strength
Early symptoms which confused us included apathy, lack of empathy, mood swings, risk taking and then serious anger and verbal aggression. Approximately, 7 years before he was diagnosed we began to ride a roller coaster of changes where he craved sweets, drank more alcohol, his handwriting deteriorating, he was aggressive and he was less and less himself. On a trip to NY to visit our daughter,he lost the car. Falls became more frequent and included falls backwards down the stairs, into things breaking ribs and many pairs of glasses. He complained of double vision while driving but only stopped when he scared himself. He had urinary retention issues, sleep became increasingly more disturbed, with him awakening 15-20 times a night. He became wheelchair bound. His preferred foods were slowly taken from him as his ability to safely swallow food was impacted. He fought
1

more frequent and longer bouts of aspiration pneumonia. He began a relationship with a woman in Louisiana who had reached out and scammed him via FB as she wanted a rich lawyer. He spent money recklessly depleting one of our retirement accounts and in August of 2015, things reached a climax. In a confrontation over missing money, he pointed a gun at me. Without this crisis point, I struggle to think of where things would have gone.
His work and profession were taken from him as well as his independence and his ability to care for himself and his family or even manage the activities of daily living without assistance. He lost the privacy of his life and home at a time when his illness created many fears; his care necessitated 24/7 help from professional agency caregivers who were strangers. As the diseases progressed his interests in technology, shopping and sharing good food became compulsive. The cardinal symptom of PSP, impaired vision, resulted in the loss of his ability to drive, problems eating as he could not see his food, inability to play chess and finally the loss of his main diversion, TV. What was thought to be joint pain and cramping from exercise, slowly became the constant pain and discomfort of dystonia for which there was no real relief. His exercise routine that he fought to maintain was adapted and modified until weeks before his passing, when he had to acknowledge that he no longer could do it. His physical isolation was compounded by his need for assistance in manipulating his phone and accessing his computer. His voice became softer and Alexa could no longer be commanded to play his favorite music. Only at the end did he lose hope of ever riding his bike daily on the Rail Trail, something that had long been his passion, his pleasure.
I am a social worker. I retired after 40 years working for SOV in child protection agency to care for Ken. I left that life to assume immediately the 24/7 job as sole family caregiver for my husband who had this complicated condition that the orthopedist said would improve with surgery, that his PCP treated each symptom without seeing the whole picture as she had never cared for someone with PSP or FTD, and an optometrist who prescribed prisms that didn't work. I had no name for this condition to Google. No one ever suggested he had PD, but suggested that his drinking caused the falls, his behavior oppositional and within his control and that aging was responsible for all the odd and assorted other things that were taking him away from me and from himself.
My only resources were my knowledge, skills, and training as a child protection social worker. I had years of experience facing unknown, unpredictable situations, dealing with life threatening crises without specific knowledge. I had research skills that I utililized nightly to try to discover what was wrong. I had years advocating and educating. I had skills to build teams. I had the ability to dissociate and compartmentalize while surrounded by anticipatory grief and the grief of bureaucratic death. I had worked for 40
2

years with those who had no voice, limited resources, facing situations beyond their control and I found myself there.
PSP is a family disease, affecting all who care for the person diagnosed. It impacts whether families are able to come together to care for the person or if the condition overwhelms. My 4 children were unable to provide much support for his care due to distance, family responsibilities and complicated feelings. For the first year, I was his sole caregiver. Shortly after his diagnosis we were then introduced to congregate living: I was in rehab for 3 weeks and he in assisted living. While he was still in assisted living we began our education regarding the world of professional caregiving. We had to hire professional caregivers to augment his care in the facility. He returned home with the recommendation we have 24/7 assistance. We met some wonderful caring people, all of whom were totally without awareness or knowledge of PSP. Their only training regarding brain disease was regarding Alzheimer's, a very different disease. It was a revolving door of people with little consistency and predictability as his physical care increased.
It required another crisis in the ED with medical staff who I had to educate about PSP and a night of them caring for him to be referred to hospice. Hospice was an incredibly caring and supportive experience, however, they had to play catch up until he died as they had never cared for someone with PSP. Days before Ken's death, while I was at his first team meeting, something I had requested at the time he was diagnosed 14 months before, we wrestled with the need support as increasing support was needed in the home and no one no one on the team could name a place in Vermont with the training and experience to care for someone with PSP.
PSP is a rare diseases that isolates and is isolating. A Resolution identifying May as PSP Awareness Month will be a significant step in beginning to raise community awareness of PSP without adding to the work of individuals impacted who are the ones who now educate, advocate and train everyone who they come in contact with. It will shine the light on brain diseases and its impact and raise awareness that there are many of these diseases as there are many types of cancer. It will make sure that those who suffer from PSP have the support wherever they live, whatever their financial circumstances, whoever their resources are. It will reflect the critical importance of collaboration among the experts, health care providers and those impacted moment to moment by these diseases. It will help to create plans where research, diagnosis, treatment and support for caregivers and a cure are addressed holistically, offering improved quality of life and perhaps a longer life. It is the first step towards a cure. This Resolution is the key to unlocking awareness. I encourage Maine to be a leader in taking this step.
Respectfully Submitted by: Janis Appel MSW, St Albans Vermont
